docs.text: Bench verification ¶ The DMA layer ( DMA ) is tested on host against kb-core's DMA-and-cache model. What a model cannot show (real caches and speculative reads, bus errors, EN-clear latency, interrupt cost, ADC overrun behaviour, MPU set-up) is verified on a board, by hand, with the bench app and the fixed evidence form here. File What procedure-stm32h7.md Step-by-step procedure for an STM32H7 board of the H743/H747 class, with the wiring and every item's hardware evidence-form.md The form a run fills in: one table per run, one row per item runs/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<board>.md Filled forms, one per run (none yet) ../../../tests/target/dma/ The bench app dma_bench (built in CI for G4, H7, F4 and L4 by the STM32 family matrix) The app prints one line per item: KB-BENCH <item> PASS|FAIL|SKIP key=value ... A run is complete when every item of the procedure has a line, the form is filled, and the console log is attached. docs.text: Bench procedure: STM32H7 ¶ For a single-core STM32H7 board of the H743 class (H743, H753, H750): a Nucleo-H743ZI2 or similar with an ST-LINK (SWD and a virtual COM port) and the pins below reachable. The dual-core parts (H745, H747, H755, H757) are refused by the port's configure step ( Integration ), so an H747 board cannot run the app until the port supports its Cortex-M7 build. What is needed ¶ Part Used by The board, one USB cable to the ST-LINK every item (power, SWD, console) One jumper wire, PB5 (SPI1 MOSI) to PA6 (SPI1 MISO) every spi-* item, t7-en-clear , spi-ovr-forced , dma-te-dtcm Two 10 kΩ resistors as a divider from 3V3 to GND, the mid point to PA3, PC0, PB1, PF11, PA0 and PA4 every adc-* item A serial terminal at 115200 8N1 on the ST-LINK virtual COM port (USART3, PD8/PD9) every item (the KB-BENCH lines) An SWD tool (OpenOCD or STM32CubeProgrammer) flashing A logic analyser on PA5, PB5, PA6, PD14 (optional) SCK rate and frame gaps of the spi-* items The ADC pins are analog at reset; the app does not change their mode. Keep the divider short (the six inputs share one mid point; each reads about 1.65 V, half of VREF+). Steps ¶ Build. From the repository root, with the Arm GNU toolchain: cmake -S examples/stm32 -B build/h7 -G Ninja -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE = cmake/arm-none-eabi.cmake \ -DKB_ARM_CORE = cortex-m7f -DEXAMPLE_BOARD = h7 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Release cmake --build build/h7 --target dma_bench sha256sum build/h7/dma_bench.elf Record the image commit, the kb-core lock commit ( third_party/kb-core.lock ), the toolchain version and the hash in the form. 2. Wire as in the figure; check the jumper and the divider with a meter (PB5-PA6 continuity, about 1.65 V at the mid point with the board powered). Tick the wiring check in the form. 3. Open the console at 115200 8N1 on the virtual COM port and start logging to docs/assurance/bench/runs/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<board>.log . 4. Flash and reset: openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32h7x.cfg -c "program build/h7/dma_bench.elf verify reset exit" . 5. Wait for KB-BENCH bench-end (about ten seconds). The app runs the items in the order of the table below, once. Do not touch the wiring meanwhile. 6. Read the silicon revision ( DBGMCU->IDCODE , for example with openocd ... -c "mdw 0x5C001000" ) and the clock tree the app ran with ( bench-start core_hz ; the app keeps the reset clock: HSI 64 MHz, SPI123 kernel clock on per_ck , the ADC on HCLK / 4). 7. CI runs kokeb-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Sending and receiving a CAN frame ¶ Sending and receiving a CAN frame Figure description and sources The driver's Send call reaches the CanController, which takes its send lock and adds the frame to a free TX FIFO element (FDCAN) or mailbox (bxCAN) through HAL CAN, sleeping for the transmit-complete interrupt when none is free. The controller sends the frame to the Other node, which acknowledges it. A frame the Other node sends lands in RX FIFO 0, and the HAL CAN receive callback moves every frame into the port's ring of 32 frames at once. The driver's Receive call takes its own receive lock and the oldest frame of the ring, waiting for the receive interrupt when the ring is empty; frames lost to a full FIFO or ring are reported as Overflow by the next Receive. Drawn from: docs/model/can-send-receive.seq.yml ; inc/kb/port/stm32/can.hpp ; src/boundary/can.cpp ; src/can.cpp . It starts HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_IT without a STOP; the HAL I2C interrupt handler sends START, the address with the write bit and the register bytes to the Device, and its completion callback wakes the task. The controller then starts HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Receive_IT, which sends a repeated START and the address with the read bit, reads the reply and ends with STOP. Both phases share one timeout on the port's clock; the controller classifies the HAL status and error code, restores the handle after a failure, runs the bus recovery when SDA or SCL stays low, and returns a kb::Status to the driver. docs.text: ADC ¶ kb::port::stm32::AdcChannel is one regular channel of an ADC and satisfies kb::iface::AdcChannel . HAL stm32<family>xx_hal_adc , single conversion, software start, ended by the end-of-conversion interrupt ( How the port waits ). How it works ¶ Call HAL call EnsureReady() The ADC clock checked (0 Hz: NotReady ; above the H7 limit: Unsupported ); the pin as analog (when given); the first channel of the instance initialises it (clock, HAL_ADC_Init , on G4 and L4 HAL_ADCEx_Calibration_Start single ended, on H7 offset and linearity, the instance's interrupt at priority 5) while the others wait at most lock_timeout ; later channels join it ReadRaw() The instance lock; HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel (the channel, rank 1, the sampling time); HAL_ADC_Start_IT ; the task waits for HAL_ADC_ConvCpltCallback (which reads HAL_ADC_GetValue ) at most conversion_timeout ; on a timeout HAL_ADC_Stop_IT ReadMillivolts() ReadRaw() scaled by vref_mv / FullScale() , rounded to nearest Release() The instance's channel count drops; the last channel de-initialises it ( HAL_ADC_DeInit ), in any order of release The instance's channel count and phase (closed, opening, open) change only with interrupts masked, so two tasks that start or release channels of one instance never initialise it twice or de-initialise it under the other. A timer-triggered scan of several ranks streamed by circular DMA is AdcDmaStream ( DMA ): it owns its instance alone (an AdcChannel on the same instance is refused with Busy , and the other way round). Inputs and clock ¶ Item Note Instance, channel ADC1 to ADC5 where the device has them; channel 0 to 19 ( ADC_CHANNEL_<n> ), 0 to 18 on F4 Pin The pin of the channel (datasheet pinout), set analog; unused for internal channels (temperature, VREFINT) Resolution 12 bit ( FullScale() 4095) on G4, F4, L4; 16 bit (65535) on H7 Reference vref_mv : the voltage on VREF+ (3300 mV default); the port does not measure VREFINT ADC clock The HAL's synchronous clock HCLK / 4 on G4, H7, L4 and PCLK2 / 4 on F4. On H7, when HCLK / 4 is above 36 MHz (the lower of the H7 revisions' limits), the asynchronous kernel clock (RCC ADCSEL, HAL_RCCEx_GetPeriphCLKFreq(RCC_PERIPHCLK_ADC) ) with the smallest of the HAL's dividers (1 to 256) that brings it to 36 MHz or less ( AdcAsyncDividerIndex() ); the HAL sets the BOOST mode from the chosen clock. The controller sends the frame to the Other node, which acknowledges it. A frame the Other node sends lands in RX FIFO 0, and the HAL CAN receive callback moves every frame into the port's ring of 32 frames at once. The driver's Receive call takes its own receive lock and the oldest frame of the ring, waiting for the receive interrupt when the ring is empty; frames lost to a full FIFO or ring are reported as Overflow by the next Receive. Bit timing ¶ ComputeCanTiming() takes the kernel clock and the bit rate and picks the most time quanta per bit (8 to 25) that divide the clock exactly with a prescaler in range, with the sample point nearest 87.5 % (CiA 301) and SJW equal to phase segment 2 (at most the controller's limit). Prescaler Seg 1 Seg 2 SJW FDCAN nominal 1 to 512 1 to 256 1 to 128 1 to 128 bxCAN 1 to 1024 1 to 16 1 to 8 1 to 4 A bit rate the clock cannot make exactly (for example 500 kbit/s from 41 MHz) is InvalidArgument ; choose a kernel clock that is a multiple of the bit rate (40, 80, 160 MHz on FDCAN; 42 or 45 MHz APB1 on F4). Timing() returns the fields in use. Pins and clock ¶ Item Note TX, RX PinId with the CAN alternate function (AF9 for FDCAN1 and CAN1 on PA11/PA12 and PB8/PB9 on most parts); RX with pull-up. A transceiver (for example a 3.3 V TCAN or SN65HVD part) is needed on the bus Kernel clock kernel_clock_hz , or 0: HAL_RCCEx_GetPeriphCLKFreq(RCC_PERIPHCLK_FDCAN) on G4 and H7, PCLK1 on F4 and L4 Bit rate 10 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s Timing limits ¶ Wait Bound The send and the receive locks lock_timeout each (default 10 ms, at most 2 s) Send Its timeout (at most 2 s) for a free slot; a bus-off controller ends the wait at once with BusError Receive Its timeout (at most 2 s) for a frame Recover Its timeout (at most 2 s) for the controller to leave bus-off, checked after each bounded pause (the send lock is held for the whole wait) Send and Receive have separate locks: a Receive() that waits does not hold off a Send() from another task. Losses ¶ RX FIFO 0 holds 3 frames on G4 FDCAN and on bxCAN (16 as the port configures it on H7). The receive interrupt empties it into the controller's ring of kCanRxFrames (32) at once, so a burst is not lost while the receiving task is busy. A FIFO overrun ( can_flags::kFifoOverrun ) or a full ring ( can_flags::kRingFull ) is latched and the next Receive() returns Overflow with the flags in Detail() ; the frames already in the ring stay for the receives that follow. docs.text: I2C ¶ kb::port::stm32::I2cController satisfies kb::iface::I2cBus over the HAL's I2C module ( stm32<family>xx_hal_i2c ), interrupt-driven transfers: the calling task waits on the port's clock for the HAL's completion callback, asleep under an RTOS ( How the port waits ). How it works ¶ Step HAL call EnsureReady() The instance clock, SCL and SDA as open-drain alternate function, then HAL_I2C_Init : Timing from ComputeI2cTiming() on G4, H7 and L4 (or I2cConfig::timing as given), ClockSpeed and duty cycle 2 on F4 Before every transfer I2C v2: a latched TXIS cleared with a dummy byte, TXDR flushed, RXDR read, the CR2 transfer fields (NBYTES, RELOAD, AUTOEND, START, STOP, RD_WRN) cleared Write(addr, tx) HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_IT (first and last frame); an empty tx is an address probe, HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit_IT of no data WriteRead(addr, tx, rx) HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_IT of tx (any length) without STOP, then HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Receive_IT of rx after a repeated START Read(addr, rx) HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Receive_IT (first and last frame) After a failure The handle back to READY and unlocked, the peripheral's interrupts off, the error flags (NACK, STOP, BERR, ARLO, OVR) cleared, the data registers flushed; if BUSY is still set, the peripheral is reset ( HAL_I2C_DeInit and HAL_I2C_Init : PE cleared; SWRST on F4) RecoverBus() HAL_I2C_DeInit , SCL and SDA as open-drain GPIO with the configured pull, up to nine SCL clocks at 100 kHz until SDA is high, a STOP, both lines read back, then HAL_I2C_Init again Release() HAL_I2C_DeInit One I2C register read Figure description and sources The driver's WriteRead call reaches the I2cController, which takes its lock within the timeout and clears stale transfer state in the peripheral. It starts HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Transmit_IT without a STOP; the HAL I2C interrupt handler sends START, the address with the write bit and the register bytes to the Device, and its completion callback wakes the task. The controller then starts HAL_I2C_Master_Seq_Receive_IT, which sends a repeated START and the address with the read bit, reads the reply and ends with STOP. Both phases share one timeout on the port's clock; the controller classifies the HAL status and error code, restores the handle after a failure, runs the bus recovery when SDA or SCL stays low, and returns a kb::Status to the driver. Drawn from: docs/model/i2c-write-read.seq.yml ; inc/kb/port/stm32/i2c.hpp ; src/boundary/i2c.cpp ; src/completion.cpp ; src/i2c.cpp . The controller owns the instance: a second I2cController on it gets Busy from EnsureReady() . Pins and clock ¶ Item Note SCL, SDA PinId with the I2C alternate function of the device (AF4 on most pins; check the datasheet). Open-drain Pull-ups External 2.2 kOhm to 4.7 kOhm to the bus voltage. internal_pullups enables the weak internal ones (about 40 kOhm): short buses at 100 kHz only Bus clock clock_hz 10 kHz to 1 MHz on G4, H7 and L4 (Fast-mode Plus needs FM+ capable pins), 10 kHz to 400 kHz on F4 Kernel clock (G4, H7, L4) kernel_clock_hz , or PCLK1 (the reset selection) when 0. TIMINGR is computed for it and must be at least 4 times the bus clock; InvalidArgument when no prescaler fits TIMINGR ComputeI2cTiming() meets the I2C specification's minimum SCL low and high times, data setup time and rise time of the mode (standard, fast, fast-mode plus); give timing to use a value from STM32CubeMX instead. Keep that override: observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware, a sensor bus computed for 400 kHz and 100 kHz returned corrupt or unapplied data on real wiring, and only a ~25 kHz timing worked until the pull-ups were changed Kernel clock 0 Hz Refused by EnsureReady() with NotReady ( kNoClock ) Interrupts I2Cn_EV and I2Cn_ER at irq_priority (default 5) Timing limits ¶ Wait Bound The controller lock I2cConfig::timeout (default 50 ms, at most kMaxTimeout = 2 s); Busy when not had, nothing is sent One transfer (a WriteRead() : both phases) I2cConfig::timeout , from the start of the transfer, on the port's clock Clock stretching Inside the transfer's budget; a longer stretch ends as Timeout F4 start The HAL waits for BUSY to clear with a counted loop (about 25 ms of iterations at the core clock), then HAL_BUSY Probe after a NACK ( nack_probe only) One more transfer budget Restore, reset Register writes; the reset is a de-initialisation and an initialisation of the peripheral Recovery ( BusStuck , auto_recover ) Nine clocks of 10 us, a STOP: about 100 us, then an initialisation Length At most 65535 bytes each way (the HAL's uint16_t ); more is InvalidArgument The worst case of one call is: lock wait (T) + transfer (T) + probe (T, only with nack_probe ) + reset and recovery (well under 1 ms), plus up to 25 ms of the F4 busy-flag loop. With the default T = 50 ms: about 100 ms (125 ms on F4), 150 ms with nack_probe . Results and failure kinds ¶ Result LastFailure() When Ok None The transfer completed NoDevice AddressNack HAL_I2C_ERROR_AF on a Read() or an empty write (only the address was sent); with nack_probe , a write whose address probe was not acknowledged Nack DataNack HAL_I2C_ERROR_AF on a write: the address or a data byte (not split without nack_probe ); with nack_probe , the probe was acknowledged, so a data byte was refused Timeout Timeout HAL_TIMEOUT with both lines high (clock stretching too long, a device that holds SCL) BusError Bus HAL_I2C_ERROR_BERR , HAL_I2C_ERROR_ARLO , HAL_BUSY (BUSY set before the start) or another HAL error, with both lines high; a BUSY that stays set resets the peripheral BusError BusStuck Any failure with SDA or SCL read low afterwards; with auto_recover (default) RecoverBus() runs at once InvalidArgument unchanged Address outside 0x08 to 0x77, an empty read, a span above 65535 bytes, a timeout above 2 s, a bad configuration Busy unchanged The lock was not had within the timeout, or the instance is owned by another object NotReady unchanged Before EnsureReady() LastError().Detail() is the vendor code: the HAL_StatusTypeDef in bits 0 to 7 and the handle's ErrorCode ( HAL_I2C_ERROR_* ) from bit 8. Stats() counts transfers, failures, recoveries and lock timeouts. Address probes ¶ The HAL reports a NACK of the address and of a data byte with one bit. The controller sends an address-only frame only when asked: an empty Write() (an explicit probe), or after a write NACK with nack_probe set. It is off by default, and EnsureReady() never probes: observed with an SE05x secure element, the device NACKs every poll while it is busy, and an address-only frame to its address can make it hold the bus (vendor errata). Drivers that need the split set nack_probe for their own controller. The BUSY flag ¶ Observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware: after an error the I2C BUSY flag can stay set with both lines idle, so the next transfer fails with HAL_BUSY until the peripheral is reset; and toggling PE after every NACK left the master unresponsive on a busy bus, while restoring the HAL state and clearing the error flags, with a PE toggle only while BUSY stays set, recovered it. The controller does exactly that after every failure, on every family (the same holds for the F4's I2C v1, where the reset is SWRST). Also observed there: a latched TXIS after HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady , and stale CR2 NBYTES/AUTOEND after a transmit, made the next combined read lose its register address; hence the flush and the CR2 clear before every transfer. Bus recovery ¶ A slave that lost a clock edge (a reset in the middle of a read, a glitch) can hold SDA low forever. After any failed transfer the controller reads SDA and SCL; when one is low the failure is BusStuck and, with auto_recover , the recovery follows at once: the peripheral is released, the pins are taken as open-drain GPIO (with the internal pull-ups kept when internal_pullups is set), SCL is clocked until the slave lets SDA go (at most nine clocks), a STOP is made and the peripheral is initialised again. The transfer itself is not retried: the caller decides. A device holding SCL low cannot be clocked free: the recovery then sends no clocks and counts it in Stats().scl_held . If the peripheral cannot be initialised again after a recovery, the controller is no longer ready: its calls return NotReady until EnsureReady() succeeds. A line still low after the recovery is reported as BusError with LastFailure() BusStuck (a short, a missing pull-up, a device in reset). docs.text: The HAL reports a NACK of the address and of a data byte with one bit. The controller sends an address-only frame only when asked: an empty Write() (an explicit probe), or after a write NACK with nack_probe set. It is off by default, and EnsureReady() never probes: observed with an SE05x secure element, the device NACKs every poll while it is busy, and an address-only frame to its address can make it hold the bus (vendor errata). Drivers that need the split set nack_probe for their own controller.

docs.text: Observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware: after an error the I2C BUSY flag can stay set with both lines idle, so the next transfer fails with HAL_BUSY until the peripheral is reset; and toggling PE after every NACK left the master unresponsive on a busy bus, while restoring the HAL state and clearing the error flags, with a PE toggle only while BUSY stays set, recovered it. The controller does exactly that after every failure, on every family (the same holds for the F4's I2C v1, where the reset is SWRST). Also observed there: a latched TXIS after HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady , and stale CR2 NBYTES/AUTOEND after a transmit, made the next combined read lose its register address; hence the flush and the CR2 clear before every transfer.
docs.title: The BUSY flag

docs.text: A slave that lost a clock edge (a reset in the middle of a read, a glitch) can hold SDA low forever. After any failed transfer the controller reads SDA and SCL; when one is low the failure is BusStuck and, with auto_recover , the recovery follows at once: the peripheral is released, the pins are taken as open-drain GPIO (with the internal pull-ups kept when internal_pullups is set), SCL is clocked until the slave lets SDA go (at most nine clocks), a STOP is made and the peripheral is initialised again. The transfer itself is not retried: the caller decides. A device holding SCL low cannot be clocked free: the recovery then sends no clocks and counts it in Stats().scl_held . If the peripheral cannot be initialised again after a recovery, the controller is no longer ready: its calls return NotReady until EnsureReady() succeeds. A line still low after the recovery is reported as BusError with LastFailure() BusStuck (a short, a missing pull-up, a device in reset).

How it works ¶ Call What EnsureReady() The timer's clock and HAL_TIM_PWM_Init the first time a channel of the timer starts (counted), the prescaler and auto-reload from ComputePwmPeriod() for frequency_hz ; the pin as alternate function; HAL_TIM_PWM_ConfigChannel and HAL_TIM_PWM_Start ; the output held at its idle level SetFrequencyHz(hz) New PSC and ARR, an update event ( HAL_TIM_GenerateEvent ); the duty is kept as a fraction SetDuty(duty) CCR = duty x (ARR + 1) / 10000, rounded to nearest Enable(on) false holds the output at idle_high by a compare of 0 or full; the counter keeps running Release() HAL_TIM_PWM_Stop ; HAL_TIM_PWM_DeInit with the last channel of the timer ComputePwmPeriod() picks the smallest prescaler whose period fits the 16-bit auto-reload, so the duty has the finest steps the timer allows (ARR + 1 steps). docs.text: SPI ¶ kb::port::stm32::SpiBus is one SPI peripheral as master; kb::port::stm32::SpiDevice is one chip select on it and satisfies kb::iface::SpiDevice and kb::iface::SpiClockControl . HAL stm32<family>xx_hal_spi , interrupt-driven transfers waited for on the port's clock ( How the port waits ), 8-bit frames, MSB first. How it works ¶ Step HAL call SpiBus::EnsureReady() The kernel clock checked (0 Hz: NotReady ); the instance clock, SCK, MOSI and MISO as alternate function (MOSI or MISO may be unused), HAL_SPI_Init in mode 0 at the slowest prescaler (/256), the instance's interrupt at irq_priority (default 5); the first frame sets its device's mode and clock SpiDevice::EnsureReady() The bus's EnsureReady() , the chip select as push-pull GPIO driven high Transfer(tx, rx) The bus lock; when another device used the bus last, CPOL, CPHA and the baud-rate prescaler are set again ( HAL_SPI_DeInit , HAL_SPI_Init : the peripheral is disabled while it is reprogrammed); CS low; HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_IT (or HAL_SPI_Transmit_IT for a write-only frame; a read-only frame clocks its zeroed receive buffer out in place with HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_IT , on every family) in chunks of at most 65535 bytes, each waited for until the HAL's completion callback; CS high, whatever the result After a timeout HAL_SPI_Abort ; the peripheral is initialised again before the next frame ( Stats().rebuilds ) SetClockHz(hz) Recomputes the prescaler; applied at the next frame SpiDevice::Release() The chip select pin back to its reset state and unclaimed SpiBus::Release() HAL_SPI_DeInit (release the devices first) One SPI frame Figure description and sources The driver's Transfer call reaches the SpiDevice, which takes the bus lock within its timeout and, when another device used the bus last, initialises the HAL SPI again with its own mode and prescaler. It drives its chip select GPIO low, starts HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive_IT, and the HAL's interrupt handler clocks the bytes to the Device and reads its reply. The task sleeps on the port's Completion until the HAL's completion callback, at most the timeout per chunk, then the SpiDevice raises chip select; a timeout aborts the transfer and the peripheral is initialised again before the next frame. A kb::Status returns to the driver. Drawn from: docs/model/spi-transfer.seq.yml ; inc/kb/port/stm32/spi.hpp ; src/boundary/spi.cpp ; src/completion.cpp ; src/spi.cpp . Chip select is a GPIO, not the peripheral's NSS: any pin can be a chip select, and CS stays low across chunks. Its idle level is written before the pin becomes an output. While the peripheral is disabled for a mode change, SCK is not driven on F4, G4 and L4 (H7 keeps it at its idle level with MasterKeepIOState ); every CS is high then, so no device sees a clock, but a pull to the CPOL level on SCK keeps the line quiet. The inter-data idleness (H7 MIDI) is the HAL default, none, for every device: observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware, a gap inside a 32-bit word desynchronised a slave, so a device that needs one is not served yet. Pins and clock ¶ Item Note SCK, MOSI, MISO PinId with the SPI alternate function (AF5 or AF6 on most pins). Push-pull, very high speed CS Any GPIO, push-pull, active low; one per SpiDevice Clock clock_hz is the highest SCK wanted; the prescaler (2, 4, ... 256) rounds down: the SCK is the fastest at or below both clock_hz and the bus's interrupt ceiling (below), so it may be lower than asked. ActualClockHz() (and Stats().actual_clock_hz ) is the SCK used; Stats().clamps counts lowered selections. InvalidArgument when even /256 is above either Kernel clock kernel_clock_hz , or 0: the instance's APB clock (SPI2 and SPI3 on APB1, the others on APB2), and on H7 the SPI kernel clock from the RCC Modes 0 to 3 (CPOL, CPHA) per device The interrupt ceiling ¶ Transfers run by the HAL's interrupt handler, which runs once for each transmit-empty and each receive-not-empty event: about 300 core cycles per byte with exception entry and exit. Without a receive FIFO (F4) a received byte must be read within one byte time, or the next one overruns it ( HAL_SPI_ERROR_OVR , reported as BusError ); with a FIFO (G4 and L4: 4 bytes, H7: 16) the handler has a few bytes of slack but must keep up on average. The SCK of every interrupt transfer is therefore limited to: Family Ceiling ( SpiInterruptCeilingHz ) Example SCK used (prescaler at or below the ceiling) F4 (no FIFO) core clock / 64 (512 cycles per byte: the handler plus room for other interrupts) 168 MHz core, SPI1 on an 84 MHz APB2: ceiling 2.625 MHz 84 MHz / 32 = 2.625 MHz G4, L4 (4-byte FIFO) core clock / 40 (320 cycles per byte) 170 MHz core and kernel: ceiling 4.25 MHz 170 MHz / 64 = 2.66 MHz 80 MHz core and kernel (L4): ceiling 2 MHz 80 MHz / 64 = 1.25 MHz H7 (FIFO: 16 bytes on SPI1 to SPI3, 8 on SPI4 to SPI6) core clock / 40 480 MHz core, 200 MHz SPI kernel clock: ceiling 12 MHz 200 MHz / 32 = 6.25 MHz The bus computes the ceiling from SystemCoreClock at EnsureReady() . A device asking for more runs at the fastest prescaler at or below the ceiling: the SCK may be lower than clock_hz . Config().clock_hz keeps what was asked; ActualClockHz() and Stats().actual_clock_hz give the SCK in use, and Stats().clamps counts the selections that were lowered. A driver or application that paces work from the SPI clock (a converter whose readout must finish within one conversion period, for example) reads ActualClockHz() after EnsureReady() and SetClockHz() , not the configured value. With the port's own interrupts a frame is not expected to overrun at the ceiling. A long critical section (FreeRTOS masks the SPI interrupt at the syscall limit in every critical section, and the port's own interrupt-masked sections), or a higher-priority interrupt, can still delay the handler past one byte time on F4 and cause an overrun, reported as BusError ( HAL_SPI_ERROR_OVR ). The ceilings are estimates from the pinned HAL's handler structure; a bench measurement per family is an open verification item (not yet done) . At the ceiling the handler takes most of the CPU for the frame's duration (at the SPI interrupt's priority): long frames are cheaper on a slower SCK, or with DMA. DMA is the way past the ceiling: with an SpiDmaLink attached ( SpiBus::AttachDma ), frames of at least its min_bytes go by DMA through the bus's staging buffers at the device's full SCK ( DMA ); shorter frames stay interrupt-driven at the ceiling. Observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware, SPI by circular DMA into non-cacheable SRAM ran at about 4.8 % of a 240 MHz core against about 28 % for the polled path, with zero errors. Not implemented: a polled path above the ceiling. A polled register loop for short frames would busy-wait at the caller's priority, which the port's wait rule excludes under an RTOS ( How the port waits ), so it is not offered. Without a receive FIFO (F4) a received byte must be read within one byte time, or the next one overruns it ( HAL_SPI_ERROR_OVR , reported as BusError ); with a FIFO (G4 and L4: 4 bytes, H7: 16) the handler has a few bytes of slack but must keep up on average. The SCK of every interrupt transfer is therefore limited to: Family Ceiling ( SpiInterruptCeilingHz ) Example SCK used (prescaler at or below the ceiling) F4 (no FIFO) core clock / 64 (512 cycles per byte: the handler plus room for other interrupts) 168 MHz core, SPI1 on an 84 MHz APB2: ceiling 2.625 MHz 84 MHz / 32 = 2.625 MHz G4, L4 (4-byte FIFO) core clock / 40 (320 cycles per byte) 170 MHz core and kernel: ceiling 4.25 MHz 170 MHz / 64 = 2.66 MHz 80 MHz core and kernel (L4): ceiling 2 MHz 80 MHz / 64 = 1.25 MHz H7 (FIFO: 16 bytes on SPI1 to SPI3, 8 on SPI4 to SPI6) core clock / 40 480 MHz core, 200 MHz SPI kernel clock: ceiling 12 MHz 200 MHz / 32 = 6.25 MHz The bus computes the ceiling from SystemCoreClock at EnsureReady() . A device asking for more runs at the fastest prescaler at or below the ceiling: the SCK may be lower than clock_hz . Config().clock_hz keeps what was asked; ActualClockHz() and Stats().actual_clock_hz give the SCK in use, and Stats().clamps counts the selections that were lowered. A driver or application that paces work from the SPI clock (a converter whose readout must finish within one conversion period, for example) reads ActualClockHz() after EnsureReady() and SetClockHz() , not the configured value. With the port's own interrupts a frame is not expected to overrun at the ceiling. A long critical section (FreeRTOS masks the SPI interrupt at the syscall limit in every critical section, and the port's own interrupt-masked sections), or a higher-priority interrupt, can still delay the handler past one byte time on F4 and cause an overrun, reported as BusError ( HAL_SPI_ERROR_OVR ). The ceilings are estimates from the pinned HAL's handler structure; a bench measurement per family is an open verification item (not yet done) . At the ceiling the handler takes most of the CPU for the frame's duration (at the SPI interrupt's priority): long frames are cheaper on a slower SCK, or with DMA. DMA is the way past the ceiling: with an SpiDmaLink attached ( SpiBus::AttachDma ), frames of at least its min_bytes go by DMA through the bus's staging buffers at the device's full SCK ( DMA ); shorter frames stay interrupt-driven at the ceiling. Observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware, SPI by circular DMA into non-cacheable SRAM ran at about 4.8 % of a 240 MHz core against about 28 % for the polled path, with zero errors. Not implemented: a polled path above the ceiling. A polled register loop for short frames would busy-wait at the caller's priority, which the port's wait rule excludes under an RTOS ( How the port waits ), so it is not offered.

docs.text: Clock, delay and log ¶ Clock ( MonotonicClock ) ¶ kb::port::stm32::Clock is a 32-bit timer (TIM2 or TIM5, both 32-bit on every supported family) counting at 1 MHz, extended to 64 bits by its update interrupt. Call What Start() Once: the timer's clock, HAL_TIM_Base_Init (prescaler for 1 MHz from the timer clock, auto-reload 0xFFFFFFFF), the counter set to 0 (a timer keeps counting across a jump from a loader), the update interrupt at irq_priority (default 1: high), HAL_TIM_Base_Start . The timer is then the clock's: a PwmChannel on it is refused ( Busy , port code kOwned ). Later calls, and other Clock objects on the same timer, return Ok ; a timer clock of 0 Hz is refused ( NotReady ) Now() One ClockSample , combined by Combine() (below) HandleClockIrq(timer) From TIM2_IRQHandler / TIM5_IRQHandler , with interrupts masked: clears the update flag and counts one wrap (every 71.6 minutes) Before Start() , Now() returns 0. The timer clock is timer_clock_hz , or the APB1 timer clock (doubled behind an APB prescaler, or HCLK with TIMPRE set where the family has it); a clock that is not a multiple of 1 MHz runs the clock slightly fast or slow (the prescaler is rounded to nearest). Why Now() never goes back ¶ A sample reads, in this order: the wrap count h1 , the counter c1 , the update flag p , the counter c2 , the wrap count h2 . The wrap interrupt clears the flag and counts the wrap with interrupts masked, so any reader sees both done or neither; the timer sets the flag on the same update event that reloads the counter. h1 != h2 : the interrupt ran inside the sample, so it is not used; a new sample is taken. (After three such samples, which needs the reader to be held off for a whole wrap period each time, one sample is taken with interrupts masked, where the interrupt cannot run.) h1 == h2 and p set: a wrap happened before the flag read and is not counted in h1 ; c2 , read after the flag, is after that wrap. The count is (h1 + 1, c2) . h1 == h2 and p clear: no uncounted wrap happened up to the flag read (the flag would still be set: the interrupt did not run), so none before c1 . The count is (h1, c1) . Each result is the true count at one of the sample's counter reads, so a later call returns a later count. The host tests check this against a model of the timer over every interleaving of the five reads with ticks and the wrap interrupt near a wrap ( tests/test_clock_read.cpp ), including the sequence that made the earlier rule (high, counter, high, flag) step forward by 2^32 us and back. The clock is the port's time source for every wait ( How the port waits ). The design follows a rule observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware: a 32-bit counter divided to microseconds wraps and breaks every elapsed-time computation unless it is extended to 64 bits first, and a timer counter keeps running across a jump from a bootloader, so it is zeroed when the clock starts. BusyWait ( BusyWait ) ¶ kb::port::stm32::BusyWait spins on the Cortex-M DWT cycle counter ( DWT->CYCCNT , enabled with TRCENA on first use, unlocked with LAR on the Cortex-M7, never written) for at least the asked microseconds at SystemCoreClock , rounded up. Waits longer than 2^30 cycles are split, so the 32-bit counter never wraps within one step. Interrupts lengthen a wait, never shorten it. Keep SystemCoreClock current ( SystemCoreClockUpdate() after a clock change). Log sinks ( LogSink ) ¶ Sink Where When nothing listens ItmLogSink ITM stimulus port 0, read through SWO by a debug probe The line is dropped at once when the ITM or port 0 is not enabled (no probe); each character waits at most 10000 polls for the port UartLogSink A port Uart ( Write() ) The line is dropped when the Uart refuses it; its write_timeout bounds the call Both write <letter> text\r\n ( E , W , I , D ) per call, cut at 160 characters ( kLogMaxLine ), from a stack buffer: no heap, no printf .

docs.text: UART ¶ kb::port::stm32::Uart is one USART, UART or LPUART1 and satisfies kb::iface::UartPort , UartBaudControl and UartTxDrain . HAL stm32<family>xx_hal_uart for the setup; both directions run in the port's own interrupt handler, and every wait is on the port's clock, asleep under an RTOS ( How the port waits ). How it works ¶ Step What EnsureReady() Checks that the HAL time base runs, then the instance clock, TX and RX as alternate function (RX with pull-up), the DE pin as GPIO driven low, HAL_UART_Init (baud, 7 or 8 data bits, parity, 1 or 2 stop bits, no flow control, oversampling 16, FIFO off), the receive and error interrupts, the NVIC line at irq_priority Receive HandleUartIrq(instance) (from the vector, see Interrupts ) reads the flags and the data register; OnInterrupt() masks the word to the data bits (a 7-bit frame's parity bit never reaches the caller), puts the byte into a ring of 256 bytes, latches overrun, framing, parity and noise errors (the error flags are always cleared) and wakes a waiting Read() Read(rx, timeout) Waits at most timeout for the first byte, then takes whatever else is in the ring (up to rx.size() ) Write(tx) Enables the transmit-empty interrupt; the handler sends byte by byte and ends the write at the last byte (with a DE pin: at transmit-complete, then DE low). Any length; the whole frame within write_timeout SetBaud(baud) Both locks, HAL_UART_Init again with the new rate; the ring is kept WaitTxDone(timeout) Done when transmit-complete is set; else waits for the transmit-complete interrupt FlushInput() Empties the ring and clears latched errors A UART request and reply Figure description and sources The driver's Write call reaches the Uart, which takes its writer lock and enables the transmit-empty interrupt; the port's UART IRQ handler then sends the frame to the Device byte by byte and completes the write at the last byte, with a DE pin at transmit-complete. The driver's Read call takes the reader lock and sleeps while the ring is empty, at most its timeout. The Device's reply arrives on RX, and the UART IRQ handler puts each byte into the port's ring of 256 bytes, latches any receive error and wakes the Read, which takes what the ring holds; the count returns to the driver. Observed with an earlier implementation on STM32H7 hardware, at 921 600 Bd with the FIFO off any interrupt-masked stretch longer than one byte time (10.8 us) overran RX; at such rates use a higher interrupt priority and keep masked sections short Timing limits ¶ Wait Bound The writer lock write_timeout (default 100 ms, at most 2 s) Write() write_timeout for the whole frame (DE included), on the port's clock; on a timeout the transmit interrupts are stopped and DE is driven low The reader lock The Read() timeout Read() Its timeout (at most 2 s), on the port's clock; the task blocks under an RTOS until a byte or an error arrives WaitTxDone() Its timeout (at most 2 s) Results ¶ Result When Ok Done ( Read : one byte or more) Timeout Read : nothing in time. Write : HAL_TIMEOUT ; WaitTxDone : not complete in time Overflow Read : the receiver overran or the ring was full since the last Read (Detail: the uart_flags mask) BusError Read : framing, parity or noise error since the last Read (Detail: the uart_flags mask) Busy The reader or writer lock was not had in time; or the instance is owned by another object InvalidArgument Empty span, baud 0, a timeout above 2 s, a bad configuration Unsupported 7 data bits without parity on F4 NotReady Before EnsureReady() ; or the HAL time base does not run ( kHalTickStopped ) Release() stops the interrupt and de-initialises the instance; the DE pin stays an output driven low (a floating DE with a pull-up would enable the RS-485 driver and hold the bus). An error is reported once, by the next Read() ; the bytes after it are returned by the reads that follow. Bytes received with a framing, parity or noise error are dropped.
